claim: Memory deficits are a hallmark of many different neurological and psychiatric conditions.
source: Memory deficits are a hallmark of many different neurological and psychiatric conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about neurological and psychiatric conditions that draws from established medical knowledge.

claim: The Rey–Osterrieth complex figure (ROCF) is the state-of-the-art assessment tool for neuropsychologists across the globe to assess the degree of non-verbal visual memory deterioration.
source: The Rey–Osterrieth complex figure (ROCF) is the state-of-the-art assessment tool for neuropsychologists across the globe to assess the degree of non-verbal visual memory deterioration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction section and represents established knowledge in neuropsychology.

claim: Manual ROCF scoring is time-consuming, slow and scores vary depending on the clinician's experience, motivation, and tiredness.
source: This manual procedure is time-consuming, slow and scores vary depending on the clinician's experience, motivation, and tiredness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the manuscript and represents known limitations of manual scoring.

claim: More than 20k hand-drawn ROCF drawings were collected from patients with various neurological and psychiatric disorders as well as healthy participants.
source: For this, we collected more than 20k hand-drawn ROCF drawings from patients with various neurological and psychiatric disorders as well as healthy participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset collected for the study.

claim: Unbiased ground truth ROCF scores were obtained from crowdsourced human intelligence.
source: Unbiased ground truth ROCF scores were obtained from crowdsourced human intelligence.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to obtain training labels for the neural network.

claim: A multihead convolutional neural network was trained and evaluated using the dataset.
source: This dataset was used to train and evaluate a multihead convolutional neural network.
evidence: This describes the machine learning approach used in the study.

claim: The model performs highly unbiased as it yielded predictions very close to the ground truth and the error was similarly distributed around zero.
source: The model performs highly unbiased as it yielded predictions very close to the ground truth and the error was similarly distributed around zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in the figures.

claim: The neural network outperforms both online raters and clinicians.
source: The neural network outperforms both online raters and clinicians.
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance metrics presented in the results section.

claim: The scoring system can reliably identify and accurately score individual figure elements in previously unseen ROCF drawings.
source: The scoring system can reliably identify and accurately score individual figure elements in previously unseen ROCF drawings, which facilitates explainability of the AI-scoring system.
evidence: This is supported by item-specific performance metrics shown in the results.

claim: The model performance was successfully replicated in a large independent prospective validation study that was pre-registered prior to data collection.
source: To ensure generalizability and clinical utility, the model performance was successfully replicated in a large independent prospective validation study that was pre-registered prior to data collection.
evidence: This is supported by the prospective validation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurological and psychiatric disorders are among the most common and debilitating illnesses across the lifespan.
source: Neurological and psychiatric disorders are among the most common and debilitating illnesses across the lifespan.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the citation to Trautmann et al., 2016.

claim: The aging of our population, with the increasing prevalence of physical and cognitive disorders, poses a major burden on our society with an estimated economic cost of 2.5 trillion US$ per year.
source: In addition, the aging of our population, with the increasing prevalence of physical and cognitive disorders, poses a major burden on our society with an estimated economic cost of 2.5 trillion US$ per year (Trautmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trautmann et al., 2016.

claim: Most neuropsychologists around the world use the Rey–Osterrieth complex figure (ROCF) in their daily clinical practice.
source: Most neuropsychologists around the world use the Rey–Osterrieth complex figure (ROCF) in their daily clinical practice (Rabin et al., 2005; Rabin et al., 2016), which provides insights into a person's non-verbal visuo-spatial memory capacity in healthy and clinical populations of all ages, from childhood to old age (Shin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rabin et al., 2005 and Rabin et al., 2016.

claim: The ROCF provides insights into a person's non-verbal visuo-spatial memory capacity in healthy and clinical populations of all ages, from childhood to old age.
source: Most neuropsychologists around the world use the Rey–Osterrieth complex figure (ROCF) in their daily clinical practice (Rabin et al., 2005; Rabin et al., 2016), which provides insights into a person's non-verbal visuo-spatial memory capacity in healthy and clinical populations of all ages, from childhood to old age (Shin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2006.

claim: A single neuropsychological division (e.g. at the University Hospital Zurich) scores up to 6000 ROCF drawings per year.
source: Our estimation revealed that a single neuropsychological division (e.g. at the University Hospital Zurich) scores up to 6000 ROCF drawings per year.
evidence: This is based on an estimation made by the authors.

claim: The ROCF test does not depend on auditory processing and differences in language skills that are omnipresent in cosmopolitan societies.
source: The ROCF test has several advantages as it does not depend on auditory processing and differences in language skills that are omnipresent in cosmopolitan societies (Osterrieth, 1944; Somerville et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Osterrieth, 1944 and Somerville et al., 2000.

claim: The ROCF test has adequate psychometric properties including sufficient test–retest reliability and internal consistency.
source: The test has adequate psychometric properties (e.g. sufficient test–retest reliability [Meyers and Volbrecht, 1999; Levine et al., 2004] and internal consistency [Berry et al., 1991; Fastenau et al., 1996]).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating these properties.

claim: The ROCF test has demonstrated to be sensitive to discriminate between various clinical populations.
source: Furthermore, the ROCF test has demonstrated to be sensitive to discriminate between various clinical populations (Alladi et al., 2006) and the progression of Alzheimer's disease (Trojano and Gainotti, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alladi et al., 2006.

claim: The ROCF test is sensitive to the progression of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Furthermore, the ROCF test has demonstrated to be sensitive to discriminate between various clinical populations (Alladi et al., 2006) and the progression of Alzheimer's disease (Trojano and Gainotti, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trojano and Gainotti, 2016.

claim: The ROCF test consists of three test conditions: Copy condition, Immediate Recall condition, and Delayed Recall condition.
source: The ROCF test consists of three test conditions: First, in the Copy condition subjects are presented with the ROCF and are asked to draw a copy of the same figure. Subsequently, the ROCF figure and the drawn copy are removed and the subject is instructed to reproduce the figure from memory immediately (Shin et al., 2006) or 3 min after the Copy condition (Meyers et al., 1996) (Immediate Recall condition). After a delay of 30 min, the subject is required to draw the same figure once again (Delayed Recall condition).
evidence: This describes the standard ROCF test procedure with citations.

claim: The current quantitative scoring system splits the ROCF into 18 identifiable elements.
source: The current quantitative scoring system (Meyers et al., 1996) splits the ROCF into 18 identifiable elements (see Figure 1A), each of which is considered separately and marked on the accuracy in both distortion and placement according to a set of rules and scored between 0 and 2 points (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyers et al., 1996 and Figure 1A showing the 18 elements.

claim: Each ROCF element is scored between 0 and 2 points based on accuracy in both distortion and placement.
source: The current quantitative scoring system (Meyers et al., 1996) splits the ROCF into 18 identifiable elements (see Figure 1A), each of which is considered separately and marked on the accuracy in both distortion and placement according to a set of rules and scored between 0 and 2 points (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and figure supplement showing scoring rules.

claim: Manual scoring of ROCF can take up to 15 min per figure.
source: Thus, the scoring is currently undertaken manually by a trained clinician, who inspects the reproduced ROCF drawing and tracks deviations from the original figure, which can take up to 15 min per figure (individually Copy, Immediate Recall, and Delayed Recall conditions).
evidence: This is a statement about the time required for manual scoring.

claim: The criteria of what position and distortion is considered 'accurate' or 'inaccurate' may vary from clinician to clinician.
source: One major limitation of this quantitative scoring system is that the criteria of what position and distortion is considered 'accurate' or 'inaccurate' may vary from clinician to clinician (Groth-Marnat, 2000; Shin et al., 2006; Canham et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting inter-rater variability.

claim: Machine-learning methods have successfully recognized visual structures in the Bender Gestalt Test and the Clock Draw Task.
source: Using machine-learning methods, such as convolutional neural networks and support vector machines, studies have successfully recognized visual structures of interest produced by subjects in the Bender Gestalt Test (Bin Nazar et al., 2017) and the Clock Draw Task (Kim et al., 2011; Harbi et al., 2016) – both are less frequently applied screening tests for visuo-spatial and visuo-constructive (dis-)abilities (Webb et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Canham et al., 2000 developed an algorithm to automatically identify 6 of 18 elements of the ROCF with great precision.
source: Canham et al., 2000 have developed an algorithm to automatically identify a selection of parts of the ROCF (6 of 18 elements) with great precision.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Canham et al., 2000.

claim: Vogt et al., 2019 developed an automated scoring using a deep neural network that reported a r = 0.88 Pearson correlation with human ratings.
source: More recently, Vogt et al., 2019 developed an automated scoring using a deep neural network. The authors reported a r = 0.88 Pearson correlation with human ratings, but equivalence testing demonstrated that the automated scoring did not produce strictly equivalent total scores compared to the human ratings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vogt et al., 2019.

claim: Vogt et al., 2019's automated scoring did not produce strictly equivalent total scores compared to human ratings.
source: More recently, Vogt et al., 2019 developed an automated scoring using a deep neural network. The authors reported a r = 0.88 Pearson correlation with human ratings, but equivalence testing demonstrated that the automated scoring did not produce strictly equivalent total scores compared to the human ratings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vogt et al., 2019.

claim: Petilli et al., 2021 proposed a novel tablet-based digital system for the assessment of the ROCF task.
source: Finally, Petilli et al., 2021 have proposed a novel tablet-based digital system for the assessment of the ROCF task, which provides the opportunity to extract a variety of parameters such as spatial, procedural, and kinematic scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Petilli et al., 2021.

claim: An average of 13.38 (sd = 2.23) crowdsource-based scores per figure was gathered.
source: An average of 13.38 (sd = 2.23) crowdsource-based scores per figure was gathered.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection process.

claim: The average human MSE over all images is 16.3.
source: The average human MSE over all images is 16.3, and the average human MAE is 2.41.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the crowdsourced scoring analysis.

claim: The average human MAE is 2.41.
source: The average human MSE over all images is 16.3, and the average human MAE is 2.41.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the crowdsourced scoring analysis.

claim: For a subset (4030) of the 20,225 ROCF images, scores conducted by different professional clinicians were available.
source: For a subset (4030) of the 20,225 ROCF images, we had access to scores conducted by different professional clinicians.
evidence: This describes the availability of clinician scores for comparison.

claim: The clinician MSE over all images is 9.25.
source: The clinician MSE over all images is 9.25 and the clinician MAE is 2.15, indicating a better performance of the clinicians compared to the average human rater.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clinician scoring analysis.

claim: The clinician MAE is 2.15.
source: The clinician MSE over all images is 9.25 and the clinician MAE is 2.15, indicating a better performance of the clinicians compared to the average human rater.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clinician scoring analysis.

claim: Clinicians perform better than the average human rater.
source: The clinician MSE over all images is 9.25 and the clinician MAE is 2.15, indicating a better performance of the clinicians compared to the average human rater.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the MSE and MAE values of clinicians versus average human raters.

claim: The multilabel classification network achieved a total score MSE of 3.56 and MAE of 1.22.
source: The multilabel classification network achieved a total score mean squared error (MSE) of 3.56 and mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.22, which is already considerably lower than the corresponding human performance.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation.

claim: The multilabel classification network performance is considerably lower than the corresponding human performance.
source: The multilabel classification network achieved a total score mean squared error (MSE) of 3.56 and mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.22, which is already considerably lower than the corresponding human performance.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the model's MSE/MAE to human performance metrics.

claim: Implementing data augmentation (DA) led to an improvement in accuracy with an MSE of 3.37 and MAE of 1.16.
source: Implementing additional data augmentation (DA) has led to a further improvement in accuracy with an MSE of 3.37 and MAE of 1.16.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the effect of data augmentation.

claim: Combining DA with test-time augmentation (TTA) leads to further improvement in performance with an MSE of 3.32 and MAE of 1.15.
source: Furthermore, when combining DA with test-time augmentation (TTA) leads to a further improvement in performance with an MSE of 3.32 and MAE of 1.15.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the combined effect of DA and TTA.

claim: The regression-based network variant led to a further slight improvement in performance, reducing the total score MSE to 3.07 and the MAE to 1.14.
source: The regression-based network variant led to a further slight improvement in performance, reducing the total score MSE to 3.07 and the MAE to 1.14.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the regression model evaluation.

claim: The best model results from combining the regression model with the multilabel classification model, leading to an MSE of 3.00 and an MAE of 1.11.
source: Finally, our best model results from combining the regression model with the multilabel classification model in the following way: For each item of the figure we determine whether to use the regressor or classifier based on its performance on the validation set (Figure 2B). Aggregating the two models in this way leads to an MSE of 3.00 and an MAE of 1.11.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the combined model evaluation, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: For the multilabel classification network, applying both DA and TTA jointly improves the model's performance.
source: During the experiments, it became apparent that for the multilabel classification network applying both DA and TTA jointly improves the model's performance (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Applying DA and TTA to the multihead regression model did not improve the performance compared to the non-augmented version of the model.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, applying these elements to the multihead regression model did not improve the performance compared to the non-augmented version of the model.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The model performance was replicated in the independent prospective validation study with MSE = 3.32 and MAE = 1.13.
source: In addition, the model performance was replicated in the independent prospective validation study (i.e. MSE = 3.32; MAE = 1.13).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the prospective validation study.

claim: After approximately 8000 images, no substantial improvements could be achieved by including more data.
source: (D) Convergence analysis revealed that after ~8000 images, no substantial improvements could be achieved by including more data.
evidence: This is a result from the convergence analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Errors made by the model are concentrated closely around 0.
source: In addition, we computed the difference between the ground truth score and predicted score revealing that errors made by our model are concentrated closely around 0 (Figure 3B), while the distribution of clinician's errors is much more spread out (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is supported by the error distribution shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The distribution of clinician's errors is much more spread out compared to the model.
source: In addition, we computed the difference between the ground truth score and predicted score revealing that errors made by our model are concentrated closely around 0 (Figure 3B), while the distribution of clinician's errors is much more spread out (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is supported by the error distributions shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The model exhibits a slight bias toward higher scores, although much less pronounced than clinicians.
source: It is interesting to note that, like the clinicians, our model exhibits a slight bias toward higher scores, although much less pronounced.
evidence: This is an observation from the error analysis.

claim: The model does not demonstrate any considerable bias toward specific figure elements.
source: Importantly, the model does not demonstrate any considerable bias toward specific figure elements.
evidence: This is supported by the item-specific MAE analysis.

claim: In contrast to the clinicians, the MAE is very balanced across each individual item of the figure.
source: In contrast to the clinicians, the MAE is very balanced across each individual item of the figure (Figure 3C, F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figures 3C and 3F showing item-specific MAE.

claim: The model exhibits a comparable MAE for the entire range of total scores, although there is a trend that high scores exhibit lower MAEs.
source: As can be seen, the model exhibits a comparable MAE for the entire range of total scores, although there is a trend that high scores exhibit lower MAEs.
evidence: This is an observation from the score-specific performance analysis.

claim: High-score images have fewer possible combinations compared to low-score images.
source: An exception are the highest scored images displaying the smallest error, which has two explanations: First, compared to low-score images, for which the same score can be achieved by numerous combinations of figure elements, the high-score images by nature do not have as many possible combinations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of high-scoring images.

claim: The dataset contains a proportionally larger amount of available training data for the high-score images.
source: Second, the dataset contains a proportional larger amount of available training data for the high-score images.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset composition.

claim: The model maintains high accuracy and generalizes well across various demographics and clinical conditions.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the model maintains high accuracy and generalizes well across various demographics and clinical conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive model performance analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Manual ROCF scoring requires training.
source: While the ROCF is one of the most commonly employed neuropsychological test to evaluate non-verbal visuo-spatial memory in clinical setting (Shin et al., 2006), the current manual scoring in clinics is time-consuming (5–15 min for each drawing), requires training, and ultimately depends on subjective judgments, which inevitably introduces human scoring biases (Watkins, 2017; Franzen, 2000) and low inter-rater reliability (Franzen, 2000; Huygelier et al., 2020; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements of manual scoring.

claim: Manual ROCF scoring depends on subjective judgments, which inevitably introduces human scoring biases.
source: While the ROCF is one of the most commonly employed neuropsychological test to evaluate non-verbal visuo-spatial memory in clinical setting (Shin et al., 2006), the current manual scoring in clinics is time-consuming (5–15 min for each drawing), requires training, and ultimately depends on subjective judgments, which inevitably introduces human scoring biases (Watkins, 2017; Franzen, 2000) and low inter-rater reliability (Franzen, 2000; Huygelier et al., 2020; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Manual ROCF scoring has low inter-rater reliability.
source: While the ROCF is one of the most commonly employed neuropsychological test to evaluate non-verbal visuo-spatial memory in clinical setting (Shin et al., 2006), the current manual scoring in clinics is time-consuming (5–15 min for each drawing), requires training, and ultimately depends on subjective judgments, which inevitably introduces human scoring biases (Watkins, 2017; Franzen, 2000) and low inter-rater reliability (Franzen, 2000; Huygelier et al., 2020; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Franzen, 2000 and Huygelier et al., 2020, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: An automated scoring system can overcome the problem of intra- and inter-rater variability.
source: Thus, an objective and reliable automated scoring system is in great demand as it can overcome the problem of intra- and inter-rater variability.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of automation.

claim: An automated system can remove a time-consuming, tedious, and repetitive task from clinicians.
source: More importantly, such an automated system can remove a time-consuming, tedious, and repetitive task from clinicians and thereby helps to reduce the workload of clinicians and/or allow more time for more patient-centered care.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of automation.

claim: Automation can support clinicians in making healthcare decisions more accurate and timely.
source: Overall, automation can support clinicians in making healthcare decisions more accurate and timely.
evidence: This is a general statement about the benefits of automation in healthcare.

claim: Deep learning has made significant headway in achieving above human-level performance on well-specified and isolated tasks in computer vision.
source: Over the past years, deep learning has made significant headway in achieving above human-level performance on well-specified and isolated tasks in computer vision.
evidence: This is a general statement about deep learning capabilities based on established knowledge.

claim: Unleashing the power of deep learning depends on the availability of large training sets with accurate training labels.
source: However, unleashing the power of deep learning depends on the availability of large training sets with accurate training labels.
evidence: This is a general principle of deep learning based on established knowledge.

claim: Over 20k hand-drawn ROCF images were obtained.
source: We obtained over 20k hand-drawn ROCF images and invested immense time and labor to manually scan the ROCF drawings.
evidence: This is a statement about the data collection effort.

claim: Electronic health records quadrupled in the US from 2007 to 2012.
source: Although electronic health records are increasingly available (e.g. quadrupled in the US from 2007 to 2012 [Hsiao et al., 2014]), challenges remain in terms of handling, processing, and moving such big data.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsiao et al., 2014.

claim: Challenges remain in terms of handling, processing, and moving big health data.
source: Although electronic health records are increasingly available (e.g. quadrupled in the US from 2007 to 2012 [Hsiao et al., 2014]), challenges remain in terms of handling, processing, and moving such big data.
evidence: This is a general statement about challenges in health data management.

claim: Data typically comes from various sources and exhibits large heterogeneity in terms of quality, size, format of the images, and quality of the labeled dataset.
source: Another important difficulty is that data typically comes from various sources and thus exhibits large heterogeneity in terms of quality, size, format of the images, and crucially the quality of the labeled dataset.
evidence: This is a general observation about data heterogeneity in machine learning.

claim: High-quality labeled and annotated datasets are the foundation of a successful computer vision system.
source: High-quality labeled and annotated datasets are the foundation of a successful computer vision system.
evidence: This is a general principle of computer vision based on established knowledge.

claim: A large pool of human internet workers was trained to score ROCF drawings guided by a self-developed interactive web application.
source: A novelty of our approach is that we have trained a large pool of human internet workers (crowdsourced human intelligence) to score ROCFs drawings guided by our self-developed interactive web application.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for obtaining ground truth labels.

claim: Each element of the figure was scored by several human workers (13 workers on average per figure).
source: Each element of the figure was scored by several human workers (13 workers on average per figure).
evidence: This is a statement about the crowdsourcing methodology.

claim: The median score was taken to derive ground truth scores, as it has the advantage of being robust to outliers.
source: To derive ground truth scores, we took the median score, as it has the advantage of being robust to outliers.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used to derive ground truth.

claim: Crowdsourcing participants with high level of disagreement (>20% disagreement) with clinician ratings were excluded.
source: To further ensure high-quality data annotation, we identified and excluded crowdsourcing participants that have a high level of disagreement (>20% disagreement) with this rating from trained clinicians, who carefully scored manually a subset of the data in the same interactive web application.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure for crowdsourced data.

claim: The twofold innovative approach combining digitization of neuropsychological tests and high-quality scoring using crowdsourced intelligence can provide a roadmap for how AI can be leveraged in neuropsychological testing more generally.
source: Importantly our twofold innovative approach that combines the digitization of neuropsychological tests and the high-quality scoring using crowdsourced intelligence can provide a roadmap for how AI can be leveraged in neuropsychological testing more generally as it can be easily adapted and applied to various other neuropsychological tests (e.g. Clock Drawing Test [Morris, 1994], Taylor Complex Figure Test [Awad et al., 2004], Hamasch 5-point test [Regard et al., 1982]).
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the approach with citations to other tests.

claim: The training dataset included data from children and a representative sample of patients exhibiting a range of neurological disorders.
source: Given that our training dataset included data from children and a representative sample of patients (see Figure 1B), exhibiting a range of neurological disorders, drawings were frequently extremely dissimilar to the target figure.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B showing demographics.

claim: The scoring system delivers accurate scores even in cases where drawings are distorted or have omissions.
source: Importantly, our scoring system delivers accurate scores even in cases where drawings are distorted (e.g. caused by fine motor impairments) or omissions (e.g. due to visuo-spatial deficits), which are typical impairment patterns in neurological patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's robustness supported by the performance analysis.

claim: The scoring system is robust against different semantic transformations (e.g. rotations, perspective change, brightness).
source: In addition, our scoring system is robust against different semantic transformations (e.g. rotations, perspective change, brightness) which are likely to occur in real-life scenarios, when the examiner takes a photo of the ROCF drawing, which naturally will lead to varying viewpoints and illumination conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model has been integrated into a tablet- (and smartphone-) based application.
source: To improve the usability of our system and guarantee clinical utility, we have integrated our model into a tablet- (and smartphone-) based application, in which users can take a photo (or upload an image) of an ROCF drawing and the application instantly provides a total score.
evidence: This describes the implementation of the model into a practical application.

claim: The application is currently in beta testing with selected clinicians in real-world settings.
source: The application is currently in beta testing with selected clinicians in real-world settings.
evidence: This is a statement about the current status of the application.

claim: The automated scoring system maintains explainability by providing visualization of detailed score breakdowns (i.e. item-specific scores).
source: Importantly, the automated scoring system also maintains explainability by providing visualization of detailed score breakdowns (i.e. item-specific scores), which is a highly valued property of AI-assisted medical decision making and key to help interpret the score and communicate them to the patient (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5 showing the application interface.

claim: The scoring is completely reproducible and facilitates valid large-scale comparisons of ROCF data.
source: The scoring is completely reproducible and thus facilitates valid large-scale comparisons of ROCF data, which enable population-based cognitive screening and (assisted) self-assessments.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of automated scoring.

claim: The current machine-based automated quantitative scoring system outperforms both amateur raters and clinicians.
source: In summary, we have created a highly robust and automated AI-based scoring tool, which provides unbiased, reproducible, and immediate scores for the ROCF test in research and clinical environments. Our current machine-based automated quantitative scoring system outperforms both amateur raters and clinicians.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative performance metrics presented in the results.

claim: Automated scoring systems can be developed to advance the quality of neuropsychological assessments by diminishing reliance on subjective ratings and efficiently improving scoring in terms of time and costs.
source: The present findings demonstrate that automated scoring systems can be developed to advance the quality of neuropsychological assessments by diminishing reliance on subjective ratings and efficiently improving scoring in terms of time and costs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The innovative approach can be translated to many different neuropsychological tests.
source: Our innovative approach can be translated to many different neuropsychological tests, thus providing a roadmap for paving the way to AI-guided neuropsychology.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: A dataset of 20,225 hand-drawn ROCF images was collected from 90 different countries.
source: For our experiments, we used a dataset of 20,225 hand-drawn ROCF images collected from 90 different countries (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2) as well as various research and clinical settings.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The large dataset spans the complete range of ROCF scores.
source: This large dataset spans the complete range of ROCF scores (Figure 1F) which allows the development of a more robust and generalizable automated scoring system.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1F showing the score distribution.

claim: The convergence analysis suggests that the error converges when approaching 10,000 digitized ROCFs.
source: Our convergence analysis suggests that the error converges when approaching 10,000 digitized ROCFs.
evidence: This is a result from the convergence analysis.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Review Board of the 'Kantonale Ethikkommission' (BASEC-Nr. 2020-00206).
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Review Board of the 'Kantonale Ethikkommission' (BASEC-Nr. 2020-00206).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All collaborators have written informed consent and/or data usage agreements for the recorded drawings from the participants.
source: All collaborators have written informed consent and/or data usage agreements for the recorded drawings from the participants.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The model performance was pre-registered prior to data collection at https://osf.io/82796.
source: To ensure generalizability and clinical utility, the model performance was replicated in a large independent prospective validation study that was pre-registered prior to data collection (https://osf.io/82796).
evidence: This is a statement about the pre-registration of the prospective study.

claim: The independent prospective validation study contained 2498 ROCF images from 961 healthy adults and 288 patients with various neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: For the independent prospective validation study, an additional dataset was collected and contained 2498 ROCF images from 961 healthy adults from and 288 patients with various neurological and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about the prospective validation dataset.

claim: With approximately 3000 images, diminishing mean MAEs are obtained.
source: With ~3000 images, we obtain diminishing mean MAEs.
evidence: This is a result from the convergence analysis.

claim: After approximately 10,000 images, no substantial improvements could be achieved by including more data.
source: After ~10,000 images, no substantial improvements could be achieved by including more data, as can be seen from the progression plot in Figure 2D.
evidence: This is a result from the convergence analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The acquired dataset is rich and diverse enough to obtain a powerful deep learning model for the task at hand.
source: From this, we conclude that the acquired dataset is rich and diverse enough to obtain a powerful deep learning model for the task at hand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the convergence analysis.

claim: Improvements to the model performance are likely to be achieved via algorithmic improvements, rather than via data-centric efforts.
source: In addition, this opens up an avenue for future research in that improvements to the model performance are likely to be achieved via algorithmic improvements, rather than via data-centric efforts.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions based on the convergence analysis.

claim: A large pool of approximately 5000 human workers was used to score ROCFs.
source: For this reason, we have harnessed a large pool (~5000) of human workers (crowdsourced human intelligence) who scored ROCFs, guided by our self-developed interactive web application (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statement about the crowdsourcing methodology.

claim: Workers were first trained by guided instructions and examples in the web application.
source: In this web application, the worker was first trained by guided instructions and examples.
evidence: This describes the training process for crowdsourcing workers.

claim: Workers rated each area of real ROCF drawings separately to guarantee a systematic approach.
source: Subsequently, the worker rated each area of real ROCF drawings separately to guarantee a systematic approach.
evidence: This describes the rating methodology for crowdsourcing workers.

claim: For each of the 18 elements in the figure, participants were asked to answer three binary questions: Is the item visible and recognizable? Is the item in the right place? Is the item drawn correctly?
source: For each of the 18 elements in the figure, participants were asked to answer three binary questions: Is the item visible and recognizable? Is the item in the right place? Is the item drawn correctly?
evidence: This describes the rating methodology corresponding to the Osterrieth scoring system.

claim: 600 images have been carefully scored manually by trained clinicians at the neuropsychological unit of the University Hospital Zurich.
source: In order to avoid taking such assessments into account, 600 images have also been carefully scored manually by trained clinicians at the neuropsychological unit of the University Hospital Zurich (in the same interactive web application).
evidence: This describes the quality control methodology.

claim: Each crowdsourcing worker rated at least two of the 600 clinician-scored images.
source: We ensured that each crowdsourcing worker rated at least two of these 600 images, which resulted in 108 ratings (2 figures * 18 items * 3 questions) to compute a level of disagreement.
evidence: This describes the quality control methodology.

claim: The ground truth for each drawing was obtained by computing the median for each item in the figure, and then summing up the medians to get the total score.
source: With this in mind, we have obtained the ground truth for each drawing by computing the median for each item in the figure, and then summed up the medians to get the total score for the drawing in question.
evidence: This describes the method for deriving ground truth scores.

claim: The identical crowdsourcing approach was used to obtain ground truth scores for the independent prospective validation study with an average of 10.36 crowdsource-based scores per figure.
source: The identical crowdsourcing approach has also been used to obtain ground truth scores for the independent prospective validation study (an average of 10.36 crowdsource-based scores per figure; minimum number of ratings = 10).
evidence: This describes the methodology for the prospective validation study.

claim: The mean empirical standard deviation of scores is 3.25.
source: The mean empirical standard deviation is 3.25.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the crowdsourced scoring analysis.

claim: Two variations of deep learning systems were implemented: a regression-based network and a multilabel classification network.
source: For the automated scoring of ROCF drawings, two variations of deep learning systems were implemented: a regression-based network and a multilabel classification network.
evidence: This describes the machine learning architectures used.

claim: The architecture consists of a shared feature extractor network and 18 parallel decision heads, one for each item score.
source: These considerations are the starting point for the architectural design of our scoring system, shown in Figure 2A. The architecture consists of a shared feature extractor network and 18 parallel decision heads, one for each item score.
evidence: This describes the neural network architecture shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The shared feature extractor is composed of three blocks.
source: The shared feature extractor is composed of three blocks, introducing several model hyperparameters: Each block consists of a 3 × 3 convolutional layer, batch normalization, 3 × 3 convolutional layer, batch normalization and max pooling with 2 × 2 stride.
evidence: This describes the neural network architecture.

claim: Data augmentation can help in making models more robust against semantic transformations like rotations or changes in perspective.
source: Second, DA can also help in making models more robust against semantic transformations like rotations or changes in perspective.
evidence: This is a general principle of data augmentation in machine learning.

claim: Each transformation was a combination of Gaussian blur, a random perspective change and a rotation with angles chosen randomly between −10° and 10°.
source: With these intuitions in mind, we randomly transformed drawings during training. Each transformation was a combination of Gaussian blur, a random perspective change and a rotation with angles chosen randomly between −10° and 10°.
evidence: This describes the data augmentation methodology.

claim: 4045 of the 20,225 ROCF drawings were set aside as a testing set, corresponding to 20% of the dataset.
source: To evaluate our model, we set aside 4045 of the 20,225 ROCF drawings as a testing set, corresponding to 20% of the dataset.
evidence: This describes the train-test split methodology.

claim: The remaining 16,180 images were used for training and validation, with 12,944 (80%) drawings for training and 3236 (20%) as a validation set.
source: The remaining 16,180 images were used for training and validation. Specifically, we used 12,944 (80%) drawings for training and 3236 (20%) as a validation set for early stopping.
evidence: This describes the train-validation split methodology.

claim: The networks and training routines were implemented in PyTorch 1.8.1.
source: The networks and training routines were implemented in PyTorch 1.8.1 (Paszke et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the implementation framework with citation.

claim: The main model was trained on drawings of size 232 × 300.
source: Our main model was trained on drawings of size 232 × 300 (see Figure 2D and below on details on the image resolution analysis), using batches of 16 images.
evidence: This describes the training configuration.

claim: Model parameters were optimized by the Adam optimizer with default parameters β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and ε = 1e−8.
source: Model parameters were optimized by the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2014) with the default parameters β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and ε = 1e−8.
evidence: This describes the optimization methodology with citation.

claim: The initial learning rate was set to 0.01 and decayed exponentially by a factor of 0.95 per epoch.
source: The initial learning rate, set to 0.01, was chosen to facilitate stable model convergence. It decayed exponentially by a factor of 0.95 per epoch, gradually reducing the step size to prevent overshooting the optimal solution during training.
evidence: This describes the learning rate schedule.

claim: Dropout rates were set to 0.3 and 0.5 in the convolutional and fully connected layers, respectively, to prevent overfitting.
source: To prevent overfitting dropout rates were set to 0.3 and 0.5 in the convolutional and fully connected layers, respectively.
evidence: This describes the regularization methodology.

claim: The dataset is imbalanced and contains a disproportionately high number of high-score drawings.
source: Since our dataset is imbalanced and contains a disproportionately high number of high-score drawings, we sampled the drawings in a way that resulted in evenly distributed scores in a single batch.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the dataset.

claim: The model was trained for 75 epochs and the weights corresponding to the epoch with the smallest validation loss were picked.
source: We trained the model for 75 epochs and picked the weights corresponding to the epoch with the smallest validation loss.
evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claim: Test-time augmentation was performed to promote robustness at test-time to slight variations in input data.
source: TTA was performed to promote robustness at test-time to slight variations in input data.
evidence: This describes the test-time augmentation methodology.

claim: Performance improvement was achieved by applying deterministic rotations along positive and negative angles on the unit circle.
source: Nonetheless, performance improvement was achieved by applying deterministic rotations along positive and negative angles on the unit circle.
evidence: This is a result from the test-time augmentation experiments.

claim: Five rotations were performed, uniformly distributed between −2° and 2°.
source: We performed five rotations, uniformly distributed between −2° and 2°.
evidence: This describes the test-time augmentation methodology.

claim: Using data augmentation significantly improves robustness against semantic transformations, particularly rotations and changes in perspective.
source: Using DA did not critically improve the accuracy, which is likely due to the fact that our dataset is already large and diverse enough. However, DA does significantly improve robustness against semantic transformations, as can be seen from Figure 5—figure supplement 1. In particular, using our DA pipeline, the model becomes much more robust against rotations and changes in perspective.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing robustness analysis.

claim: The scoring system is highly robust for realistic changes in rotations, perspective, brightness, and contrast of the images.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that our scoring system is highly robust for realistic changes in rotations, perspective, brightness, and contrast of the images (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5 showing robustness analysis.

claim: Performance is degraded only under unrealistic and extreme transformations.
source: Performance is degraded only under unrealistic and extreme transformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the robustness analysis.

claim: ROCF images in the dataset have varying resolutions, ranging from 100 × 140 pixels to 3500 × 5300 pixels.
source: The ROCF images in our dataset have varying resolutions, ranging from 100 × 140 pixels to 3500 × 5300 pixels.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the dataset.

claim: Inputs of size 232 × 300 yielded the best performance for both the model with and without data augmentation.
source: We observed this in our experiments which showed that inputs of size 232 × 300 yielded the best performance, both for the model with and without DA (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the image resolution analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All subsequent analyses were performed with images of size 232 × 300.
source: Thus, all subsequent analyses were performed with images of size 232 × 300.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for all analyses.
